body_markdown:
The NHS App is introducing prescription-ready notifications to help patients across England avoid unnecessary pharmacy trips. Find out how the new service works.


## NHS Introduces New Prescription Alerts to Make Pharmacy Visits Easier


Millions of people who use the NHS App could benefit from a new digital service designed to make collecting prescriptions easier and more convenient. The latest update will allow eligible users to receive notifications on their smartphones or smartwatches when their medication is ready for collection.


The initiative aims to reduce unnecessary journeys to pharmacies, save patients valuable time and help pharmacy teams manage their workloads more efficiently.


The service is being introduced across participating pharmacies in England, including branches located within major retailers such as Boots and Asda. Patients who regularly collect repeat prescriptions could find the new feature particularly useful, as it will help them know when to visit their local pharmacy.


Rather than repeatedly checking the NHS App or contacting a pharmacy by telephone, users can receive an alert when their prescription is ready.


The change forms part of the NHS's wider efforts to improve digital healthcare services and make everyday interactions with the health service more straightforward.


## How Will the New NHS Prescription Notification System Work?


The new NHS App prescription alerts are designed to give patients timely information about their medication.


Once the service is available through a participating pharmacy, eligible patients can receive a notification when their prescription is ready to collect. These alerts may appear on a connected mobile phone or smartwatch, depending on the user's device and notification settings.


The main objective is simple: help patients avoid visiting a pharmacy before their medication is available.


For example, someone who submits a repeat prescription may previously have travelled to their local chemist only to discover that the medication was still being prepared. With prescription-ready notifications, they can wait for confirmation before making the journey.


This could be particularly beneficial for people with busy work schedules, parents managing family responsibilities, older patients and those who need to collect several prescriptions regularly.


The service is also expected to reduce the number of calls pharmacies receive from people checking whether their medication is ready. By reducing these routine enquiries, pharmacy staff may have more time to support patients with medication advice and other healthcare needs.


However, patients should remember that the availability of notifications depends on their pharmacy participating in the service and the relevant digital settings being enabled.


## How to Turn On NHS App Notifications


Patients who want to receive prescription-ready alerts should check their NHS App settings.


Here is how to get started:


1. Open the NHS App on your smartphone.
2. Sign in to your account if prompted.
3. Check the app's settings and notification preferences.
4. Enable push notifications if they are switched off.
5. Make sure notifications are also permitted in your phone's settings.
6. Check the app for prescription updates and follow any instructions provided.


If you use a smartwatch connected to your phone, notifications may also appear on your watch, depending on your device settings.


It is worth noting that enabling notifications does not necessarily mean every prescription will generate an alert. The pharmacy must support the service, and the notification will depend on the information available through the system.


If you are unsure whether your local pharmacy participates, contact the pharmacy directly or check the information available through the NHS App.


Patients should continue following their usual prescription arrangements until they receive confirmation that their medication is ready.


## Which Pharmacies Will Offer the New Service?


The prescription notification rollout covers participating pharmacies across England, including locations within well-known high street and supermarket retailers.


Boots and Asda pharmacies are among the locations mentioned in reports about the expansion.


According to the supplied report, the service is expected to cover nearly 2,500 pharmacies in England. The report also describes the wider initiative as benefiting millions of NHS App users.


These figures should be understood in the context of a phased rollout. Not every pharmacy will necessarily offer the feature immediately, and availability may vary by location.


Patients should therefore avoid assuming that their local chemist is already connected to the system.


The NHS has also been developing prescription tracking features that allow users to see updates such as when medication is ready for collection or when a pharmacy has dispatched an order for delivery.


These tracking tools complement the new notifications by giving patients greater visibility over the prescription process.


## Why the NHS Is Introducing the Change


The new prescription alerts are part of a broader effort to use digital technology to improve access to NHS services.


Health Innovation Minister James Frith described the initiative as a practical example of how technology can improve people's everyday experiences while reducing unnecessary calls and freeing up pharmacy staff to focus on patient care.


NHS England's chief digital, data and technology officer, Rob Thompson, also highlighted the potential benefits of making prescription information easier to access.


The idea is to give patients more control over managing their healthcare while reducing routine administrative tasks for pharmacy teams.


Pharmacies regularly deal with enquiries from patients who want to know whether prescriptions have arrived, whether medicines are being prepared or when collection will be possible. Although these questions are understandable, answering them takes time that could otherwise be spent helping patients.


Automated notifications could reduce some of this pressure, particularly during busy periods.


The change also reflects the growing role of digital services in routine healthcare, from ordering repeat prescriptions to accessing health information and tracking medication requests.


## What Does the Change Mean for Patients?


For patients, the biggest potential benefit is convenience.


Instead of making repeated calls or travelling to a pharmacy without confirmation, users can receive an alert and plan their visit accordingly.


This may help people avoid wasted journeys, particularly if they live far from their pharmacy or have limited time to collect their medication.


The service could also make prescription collection less stressful for people who rely on regular medicines and need to organise their schedules around pharmacy opening hours.


Nevertheless, notifications should be treated as an additional source of information rather than a replacement for all existing communication methods.


Smartphone access, internet connectivity, app settings and pharmacy participation can affect whether a patient receives an alert. Notifications may also be delayed or missed.


Anyone who needs urgent clarification about a prescription should contact their pharmacy or healthcare professional rather than relying solely on a mobile notification.


## Will Patients Still Be Able to Get Prescription Information Without the App?


Digital services can make healthcare more convenient, but not everyone uses a smartphone or feels comfortable managing their healthcare online.


People who do not use the NHS App should still check the arrangements available through their pharmacy and NHS services.


The Patients Association has emphasised the importance of giving people greater choice and convenience while ensuring that non-digital ways of accessing information and support remain available.


Patients who prefer telephone contact or in-person assistance should ask their pharmacy about the options available to them.


The goal of digital improvements should be to make healthcare easier to navigate, not to leave people behind because they cannot or do not wish to use an app.


## Conclusion: A Practical Update for NHS App Users


The introduction of prescription-ready notifications represents another step towards a more convenient digital NHS experience.


By alerting patients when medication is ready for collection, the service could help reduce unnecessary pharmacy visits, cut routine telephone enquiries and give pharmacy staff more time to focus on patient care.


For NHS App users, the most practical step is to check notification settings and confirm whether their local pharmacy supports the feature.


Although the rollout will not necessarily be available everywhere at once, the initiative has the potential to make prescription collection simpler for millions of people across England.


As digital healthcare services continue to develop, the priority will be ensuring that patients can access accurate information conveniently, while preserving alternative ways to get support when needed.


**Disclaimer:** This article is for general informational purposes only and is not official NHS guidance. Pharmacy participation, notification availability and rollout dates may vary. Check the NHS App, contact your local pharmacy or consult official NHS channels for the latest information. Do not delay necessary medication or urgent healthcare advice while waiting for a notification.
